newsitem.title: USA: Rubin sees substantial child, education tax credit.
newsitem.headline: Rubin sees substantial child, education tax credit.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Friday that tax cuts emerging from upcoming U.S. budget negotiations will likely center on breaks for the middle class, though he added that relief from capital gains and estate taxes are also likely.
But he repeatedly declined to specify what kind of cuts the White House would like to see in capital gains and estate taxes.

"It seems to me likely ... that you'll have a substantial child tax credit. If you take a substantial child tax credit and you add together the educational tax credit, if it works out that way, that will be the bulk of the money that's spent on tax cuts," Rubin told a briefing.
"I think it is likely that you will have both capital gains and estate tax provisions in this legislation," Rubin said, "Beyond that, I don't think anybody can say what the specifics will be."
He added that the White House had placed no conditions on talks to reduce the capital gains tax, which Republicans have sought over Democratic objections for years.

Rubin asserted that since both Democrats and Republicans have advocated a $500 per child tax cut, it was likely to happen. When combined with proposed education incentives, the upcoming budget should offer relief primarily to the middle class, he added.

The budget accord reached Thursday night between White House and Congressional negotiators includes $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years, including $35 billion in relief for post-secondary education.
Both sides have proposed tax credits of $500 per child.
